e.t: Abenner is a proper name identifying a person. It is not a common noun describing an object, quality, or action, but a personal designation used in the Greek Old Testament. The name appears once in the LXX, at 2 Samuel 2:14. Since the verse text is not included here, its particular role in that passage cannot be described further; the lexical meaning available is simply the personal name “Abenner,” also represented as “Avenner.”

This word is a proper name for a person, rendered as “Adōniram” or “Athoniram.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general object; it identifies an individual by name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in five separate verses. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context, but its basic meaning is the person’s name itself.

This adjective means “without observation”: something not seen, noticed, or witnessed. It describes what escapes observation rather than naming an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:18. Because the verse text is not included here, its exact force in that sentence cannot be expanded beyond this basic sense. Its central idea is absence of observation—something happening or existing without being seen or noticed.

Aisimōth, also rendered Esimoth, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once in the LXX, at Numbers 33:49. Because no verse text or broader contextual evidence is available here, the name itself does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its meaning is therefore best stated as the proper name Aisimōth or Esimoth.

This adjective describes something that has not been worked up, shaped, or brought into finished form. It can therefore point to what remains unformed rather than completed. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Psalm 138:16, and its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central sense is clear: something still lacking the work or formation needed to become finished.

This adjective describes someone or something using a strange tongue—that is, speaking in a language unfamiliar to the hearers. It points to speech marked by linguistic difference, not merely unusual wording or manner. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, once in Ezekiel 3:6 and once in Baruch 4:15. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains language that sounds foreign or unfamiliar.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Ammadi” or “Ammathi.” It is a Greek LXX name rather than a general term describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 30:28. Since the available information gives the name and reference but not the verse text, its particular significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding context. The name itself does not provide a broader definition beyond identifying the individual.

This Greek LXX verb means “flare up”: to blaze, brighten, or become suddenly more intense. It describes an action or change in which something rises into a stronger, more visible state. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, including Job, Isaiah, Amos, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force—whether referring to light, fire, or another rising intensity—depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains a sudden increase or renewed brightness.

This adjective describes someone who is obstinate—stubbornly refusing to yield, listen, or change. It presents a person as resistant rather than willing to respond or follow direction. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs five times: four occurrences are in Old Testament books and one is in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains a settled, resistant unwillingness to respond. The word is therefore used of a person characterized by stubborn resistance.

This Greek LXX noun means “baggage”: the personal belongings, supplies, or equipment that people carry when traveling or moving. It refers to a person’s collected possessions rather than to the traveler himself. The word appears 31 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it describes a familiar practical part of journeys, departures, and movement. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on what the surrounding passage says about the people and possessions involved.

Arbeseer, also rendered Arveseer, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Zechariah 7:2. Because it functions as a personal or place name in the text, its ordinary meaning is its identifying name, while its precise referent depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Scripture does not provide enough information here to expand the name into a separate definition or spiritual concept.

This Greek LXX verb means “accommodate” or “please”: it describes acting in a way that meets another person’s wishes or proves acceptable to them. It can refer to seeking someone’s favor, responding agreeably, or arranging matters to suit a person or group. The word occurs 47 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used across many kinds of situations rather than being limited to one setting.

Asadias is a personal name, also rendered Asathias. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs once, in Baruch 1:1. The available wording preserves the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the person’s role or significance. Its precise importance in that passage therefore belongs to the surrounding context, while its basic lexical function is simply to designate a named person.

Asoub, also rendered Asuv, is a proper name referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs four times, all in Nehemiah. The available references identify its appearances in Nehemiah 3:11, 3:23, 10:24, and 11:15, but the name’s particular identity and role in each passage require the surrounding verse context. Its normal meaning is therefore the personal name Asoub or Asuv.

This adverb means “forthwith; straightway”—something happens immediately or without delay. It marks an action as taking place at once, rather than after waiting or preparation. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its role is therefore simple and direct: it tells the reader that the action or event being described follows promptly. The surrounding verse determines exactly what happens, but the word itself emphasizes immediacy.

This word is a proper name for the place called “Baithleem” or “Vethleem.” It identifies a specific location rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 27 times across 26 verses, from Genesis through Nehemiah. Its repeated appearance in historical and narrative books shows that it functions as a place-name used to identify where events or people are located, while the precise significance of any particular mention depends on its surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX adjective means “weighty” or “heavy.” It describes something having substantial physical weight, and it can also characterize a burden or matter as weighty when the surrounding sentence uses it that way. The word appears 35 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of passages. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.h: Make to Mount or Lift Up
e.t: The Greek Old Testament verb means “make to mount; lift up.” It describes an action that causes someone or something to climb onto a place or be raised upward. As a verb, it expresses what one person or agent does rather than naming an object or quality. This word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Leviticus. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea is causing ascent or elevation.

This word is a proper name rendered “Galaadi” or “Galaathi.” It identifies a particular named individual or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 26:33. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s precise role in that passage cannot be stated beyond its use as a specific name. “Galaadi” and “Galaathi” are two approved renderings of the same name.

gl: at least then; at any rate
d: at least then; at any rate

e.t: This Greek LXX particle means “at least then” or “at any rate.” It adds emphasis or marks a conclusion, narrowing attention to one point that can be affirmed even if other matters remain uncertain. In ordinary English, it may help express the sense of “at least,” “in any case,” or “then,” depending on the sentence. It occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, all in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “say”: it describes expressing words aloud or making a statement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Exodus and Joshua, so its basic meaning is straightforward rather than a broad description of speech, argument, or proclamation. The surrounding verse determines who is speaking and what is being said, but the word itself points simply to the act of saying something.

This word means “ten,” the number following nine and preceding eleven. It functions as a number, identifying a quantity or count in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings. It appears 275 times in this LXX corpus, so its meaning is consistent and straightforward rather than tied to one special passage. The surrounding words determine what is being counted, but the number itself remains ten.

This LXX verb means “sit down apart” or “relieve oneself,” referring to withdrawing to a separate place for bodily relief. It describes a physical action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 23:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a discreet act of sitting apart for relief.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to refute utterly—to completely disprove or decisively expose something as false. It describes forceful rejection of a claim, charge, or position rather than a mild disagreement. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Isaiah and once in Micah. Its precise force in either passage is determined by the surrounding verse and argument, but its central idea remains complete and decisive refutation.

This noun means “annoyance”—something that causes displeasure, trouble, or irritation. It names an unpleasant burden or disturbance rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, the word occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a source of vexation or discomfort.

Ezri is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears once, at Nehemiah 11:15. The available wording identifies the name simply as “Ezri,” so no broader lexical meaning is attached to it here. Its specific role in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included in this word-level entry.

This verb means to “drag” or “draw,” describing the act of pulling something along or bringing it toward oneself. It expresses a deliberate pulling action rather than simply carrying or moving something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 9:30, but the word’s basic sense remains this straightforward idea of pulling or drawing. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name: “Elkesaios” or “Elkeseos.” It identifies a person. The available lexical information does not indicate a broader quality, action, or general idea. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Nahum 1:1. Thus, readers should understand it as a personal designation rather than an ordinary descriptive word; its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse context.

This noun refers to “that which embraces”—something that surrounds, holds, or enfolds. It names an embracing object or means rather than the action itself. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 4 Maccabees 13:21; the available lexical information establishes its central meaning, but the verse text would be needed to explain precisely what is being described there.

This verb means “utterly ruin”: to bring something to complete destruction or collapse. It describes an action that leaves the object ruined rather than merely damaged or changed. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs 208 times, making it a recurring word for decisive destruction across that corpus. Its exact object and the reason for the ruin must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX conjunction means “since” or “otherwise.” It connects one statement with another by giving a reason or by presenting what would happen under a different condition. In ordinary reading, “since” introduces a basis for what follows, while “otherwise” marks an alternative consequence. The word occurs 34 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its exact force depends on how it links the surrounding statements. It is a connecting word rather than a name for a person, object, action, or quality.

This Greek LXX verb means “divide up”: to separate something into distinct portions or groups. It describes an action of arranging or distributing parts rather than leaving them together. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis 33:1. That single occurrence establishes its basic lexical sense, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly what is being divided and why. Its verbal function presents division as an action taking place.

This verb means to “drop asleep over,” describing sleep that comes upon someone or overtakes them. It presents falling into sleep rather than simply being in a settled state of sleep. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Proverbs 6:4. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is the onset of sleep coming over a person.

This noun means “pouring,” referring to the act or process of causing liquid to flow or be spread out. It presents pouring as an action or occurrence rather than naming the liquid itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Job 37:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of pouring. This word should therefore be understood as a noun describing liquid being poured or spread, not as a general term for every kind of movement or change.

This Greek LXX noun means “love,” describing love as a subject or reality rather than expressing an action by itself. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, both times in Proverbs. The word’s basic sense is therefore affection or love, while the surrounding sentence determines how that love is being discussed. Its occurrences are Proverbs 7:18 and Proverbs 30:16. As a noun, it names what is loved or felt rather than serving as a verb for loving.

This word means “good tidings,” referring to news or a message that brings favorable information. It is a noun, so it names the announcement itself rather than the act of announcing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all in six verses across 2 Samuel and 2 Kings. The surrounding passages determine what particular news is being reported, but the word’s basic sense remains favorable tidings or good news. Its earliest listed occurrence is in 2 Samuel 4:10, and its latest is in 2 Kings 7:9.

This verb means “zesty,” expressing a lively or energetic quality. It describes something as having active vigor rather than simply naming an object or person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: three occurrences are in the Old Testament and one is in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

Zogora is a proper name rendered as “Zogora”; the available information does not provide a broader lexical meaning beyond this name. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), it occurs twice, once in Genesis 13:10 and once in Jeremiah 31:4. Because it is a name rather than a common noun or action word, its particular referent must be identified from the surrounding verse and passage.

Iaddai is a personal name, also rendered Iaththe. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 27:21. Because the name appears only in that single passage and no verse text is provided here, its specific role in that verse must be understood from the surrounding context. Its basic meaning is therefore the individual name itself: Iaddai or Iaththe.

This verb means “heal”: to restore someone from sickness, injury, or bodily distress. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for healing carried out by God or occurring through his power, and it can describe a person or people being made well. The word occurs 58 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, with frequent use in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Psalms, and Hosea. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Ierim is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a descriptive word with a broader definition. In this LXX corpus, Ierim occurs twice, both times in 1 Samuel 15:3 and 1 Samuel 15:8. The supplied lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide enough verse text to explain the specific identity or role associated with Ierim in those passages.

Iesiel, also rendered Iesil, is a personal name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 11:47. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional definition or explain its name-giving significance. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being identified there.

Ιουδιν is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, represented by the forms “Ioudin” and “Iuthin.” It identifies a person rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. The name occurs five times in the Greek LXX, across four verses, appearing once in Genesis and four times in Jeremiah. Because it is a personal name, its precise identity and significance depend on the surrounding passage where it appears.

This word is a personal name, rendered as “Iōathan” or “Ioathan.” It identifies people rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times: four times in Judges and once in 1 Chronicles. Because it is a name, its precise identification depends on the surrounding passage and family or historical setting. The name appears in Judges 9 and 1 Chronicles 3, but the name itself carries no additional meaning beyond identifying the person named.

This Greek LXX verb means “fitting,” describing what is suitable or appropriate in a situation. It presents an action, arrangement, or response as fitting rather than focusing on a person or object by itself. The word occurs 25 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used in varied settings. The surrounding verse determines what is considered fitting in each case.

This verb means “make new”: it describes bringing something into a renewed or fresh condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it is used five times, including passages from Isaiah, Zephaniah, Wisdom, and the Maccabees. The word focuses on the act of renewing or making something new rather than merely naming a new object. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being renewed and the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “bind up” or “bandage,” describing the act of wrapping or securing something, especially as one would bind a wound. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek text of Sirach, in Sirach 7:8 and Sirach 30:7. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the physical act of binding up or dressing something.

This verb means “besprinkle”: to sprinkle something lightly over or across a person or object. It describes an action in which scattered drops or particles are applied rather than poured out heavily. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs six times, from Esther through 2 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on what is being sprinkled and the surrounding context.

gl: tell lies against; speak falsely of
d: tell lies against; speak falsely of

e.t: This verb means to “tell lies against” someone or to “speak falsely of” them. It describes false speech directed against another person, rather than merely making an inaccurate statement. As a verb, it expresses the action of misrepresenting someone through deceitful words. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Wisdom 1:11. Its precise force in that passage is best understood with the surrounding verse text.

This Greek LXX noun means “theft”—the taking of another person’s property unlawfully. It names the act itself rather than the person who commits it. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Genesis and Exodus, where it belongs to language about stolen property and responsibility for loss. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the wrongful taking of what belongs to someone else.

This word means “coriander,” the name of a plant. It is a noun used in the Greek Septuagint (LXX) to identify coriander as a recognizable thing, rather than to express an action, quality, or relationship. It occurs three times in the LXX, in Exodus 16:14, Exodus 16:31, and Numbers 11:7. Its precise significance in any one passage comes from that passage’s surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX noun means “small cup,” referring to a small drinking vessel. It appears once in the Greek text of the Old Testament, in Esther 1:7. The basic meaning is therefore concrete and simple: a small cup used for drinking. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself does not describe a person, action, or spiritual quality. It names the vessel.

This Greek LXX noun means “village,” referring to a small settled community rather than a major city. It can describe villages as places or groups of settlements. The word occurs 71 times in the Greek LXX, chiefly in Old Testament passages, with especially frequent use in Joshua for named locations and territorial descriptions. Its basic meaning remains consistent: a village or collection of villages within a land or region.

This Greek LXX adverb means “privately,” describing something done away from public view or without others knowing. It modifies an action by showing that the action takes place in a concealed or personal setting, rather than openly. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented in this corpus. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “stone,” referring to a naturally occurring rock or a worked stone used as an object. It is a noun and can describe a single stone or stones in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. The word occurs 285 times in this LXX corpus, showing broad use for ordinary physical stones rather than a narrow or specialized idea. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “grief,” referring to deep sorrow or distress. As a noun, it names the painful condition itself rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, including passages in Genesis, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its 40 occurrences show that it can describe sorrow as a broad human experience. The surrounding verse determines whether the grief arises from loss, hardship, correction, or another cause.

Manachath is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, in Genesis 36:23 and 1 Chronicles 1:40. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding genealogical context, but its basic function is to identify Manachath rather than express a general concept.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Misor.” It functions as a designation rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears seven times in the Greek Old Testament, across seven verses, with most occurrences in Joshua and additional occurrences in Deuteronomy and Jeremiah. Since it is a name, its precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage rather than by a broader dictionary meaning.

“Nathaniou” or “Nathaniu” is a proper name referring to a person, rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times, in two books: 2 Kings and Jeremiah. The available references identify where this personal name occurs, but the name itself does not provide enough information to explain each person’s role or circumstances. Its specific significance in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative.

This proper noun means Netophathite, identifying a person by connection with Netophath. It functions as a personal designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or spiritual condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in two passages in 2 Samuel and once in 2 Kings. The English rendering Netophathite confirms the same identifying sense, while the precise person referred to depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Nomba, also rendered Nomva, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs four times, all in 1 Samuel: 21:2 and 22:9, 11, and 19. Since no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the name itself is the clear meaning available; its particular role in each passage must be understood from the surrounding account.

This adjective describes something that brings destruction or is destructive. It identifies a harmful force, agent, or quality by emphasizing the destructive result it produces. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, in 4 Maccabees 8:19. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic meaning remains centered on causing ruin or destruction.

This verb means “of one mind; agree together.” It describes people sharing the same mind or coming into agreement rather than acting in opposition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Leviticus, Esther, and Daniel. Its basic sense focuses on unity of thought or purpose, while the surrounding verse determines what the agreement concerns. The word is therefore used for people who act in harmony or stand together in agreement.

Orniou, also rendered Orniu, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or named figure in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 2:46. The available lexical information establishes the name itself, while the verse and its surrounding context are needed to identify the person and explain his role in that passage.

This adjective describes someone or something as “all-powerful” or “all-mighty,” pointing to complete and unlimited power. It identifies the one being described by this quality rather than naming an action or an object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:22. The surrounding verse determines how the description is applied, but the word itself plainly presents the subject as possessing all might.

This Greek LXX noun refers to “that which is spread before”—something laid out or placed in front of someone. Its wording names an object or arrangement, not an action. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at Amos 2:8. The precise reference-level sense depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains something spread out before someone.

This Greek LXX verb means “draw aside; pervert.” It describes turning something or someone away from a proper direction or course, rather than leaving it as it should be. As a verb, it expresses an action of diverting or distorting. It occurs four times in the Greek text of Sirach, in four verses ranging from Sirach 4:1 to Sirach 29:8. The surrounding wording determines whether the emphasis is on pulling aside or on twisting what is right.

This noun means “battle by land”—a fight conducted on the ground rather than at sea. It names the kind of military conflict being discussed, not a person or an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 17:24. The available lexical meaning identifies the word’s central sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific situation in which it appears.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an armlet or bracelet, a piece of jewelry worn around the arm or wrist. It names a physical adornment rather than an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, in Exodus, Numbers, and Isaiah. Its central meaning remains the same across these occurrences: a decorative band or ornament worn on the arm. [p03:word:lxx:L710306:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L710306:occurrences]

This Greek LXX adjective describes something “moving round” or “surrounding.” It points to circular motion or to something positioned around another thing, rather than merely being nearby. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here: once in Ezekiel and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is movement around something or an enclosing position.

This verb means to “turn sideways”—to move or position something in a sideways direction rather than straight ahead. It describes an action, not a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 14:5. The word’s basic sense is therefore a simple change of direction or position, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is turning and why.

This noun means “fullness” or “fulfillment”—the state of being complete, filled, or brought to its intended measure. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe completeness or the full extent of something, while its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs 15 times across 13 verses in this Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages from Psalms, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Songs. These uses present a broad idea of fullness rather than a narrow reference to one particular object or action.

gl: full of thought; full of cares
d: full of thought; full of cares

e.t: This noun describes someone or something “full of thought; full of cares.” It refers to a state marked by an occupied, concerned mind rather than naming an action or command. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 9:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to being weighed down or filled with thoughts and cares.

This Greek LXX noun means “appearance” or “aspect”—the way someone or something looks or presents itself. It can describe visible form or outward character without, by itself, explaining the deeper reality behind that appearance. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, chiefly in Daniel, with one occurrence in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject.

This Greek LXX verb means “loosed beforehand; extended.” It describes an action involving something being released in advance or lengthened, depending on the sentence. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 10:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense centers on releasing something ahead of time or extending it.

Raphidin is a proper name preserved in English as “Raphidin”; “Rhafithin” is also given as a form of the name. It is a Greek LXX name rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs five times in the LXX, in Exodus and Numbers, including references to Exodus 17 and Numbers 33. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means a “club” or “cudgel,” a short, heavy object used as a striking weapon. It is a noun naming the object itself, rather than an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Proverbs 32:18, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains a solid implement used to strike or beat.

Sarira is a proper name, not a common word that describes an action, quality, or object. Its recorded meaning is simply “Sarira,” so the name itself does not provide an additional definition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, all within three verses in 1 Kings. The particular person or referent associated with the name must be identified from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

Sasabasar, also given as Sasavasar, is a personal name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament text, it occurs four times, all in Ezra, so its meaning is the identification of a person by name rather than a general vocabulary concept. The available passages preserve the name in transliterated form, without an additional descriptive definition or broader thematic sense.

This word means “beer” or “fermented liquor,” referring to an alcoholic drink. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament for a beverage that can be consumed or prohibited, depending on the passage. The word occurs 13 times in 11 verses in the LXX, from Leviticus through Isaiah. Its basic sense remains the drink itself; the surrounding passage determines whether the text describes its use, abstinence from it, or its place among ordinary beverages.

Souni, also rendered Suni, is a proper name for a person. It functions as a personal name rather than as a description, action, or general spiritual term. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both instances appearing in Numbers 26:24. The available reference identifies its location, while the name itself supplies the person’s designation. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogical context.

This word describes something round or spherical. It is a noun used to identify the shape of an object rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Kings 7, at 1 Kings 7:10 and 1 Kings 7:21. Its basic meaning remains focused and concrete: something having a rounded shape. The English rendering “round” expresses this central sense.

This verb means to “cover” or “hide”—to place something out of sight or keep it concealed. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its precise force depends on what is being covered or hidden in the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 19:27. That single occurrence identifies its normal lexical sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific action there.

This Greek LXX verb means “agree”: to be of one mind or reach agreement with others. It describes people whose views, intentions, or decisions come into harmony. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Genesis, 2 Kings, Isaiah, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains agreement or shared consent.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “slaughter”—the killing of animals or people, especially in a setting of sacrifice, judgment, or violent death. It describes the act or event of being put to death rather than a person who performs it. The word occurs 23 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including the Greek text of the Deuterocanonical books. Its repeated use in prophetic and wisdom writings gives it a serious, forceful sense connected with death and destruction, while the surrounding passage determines its precise setting.

Sōphēra, also given as Sofira, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or idea. It functions as a personal or identifying name in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs twice in the LXX corpus, in Genesis 10:30 and 1 Kings 9:28. The name itself does not provide a broader lexical meaning beyond identifying the named entity in each passage.

Tapheth, also rendered Tafeth, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, with occurrences in 2 Kings and Jeremiah. Its meaning is therefore primarily its identifying name, and the surrounding verse is needed to explain the significance of what or whom it names. The supplied renderings preserve the name as “Tapheth.”

e.h: A Word for Do For The Third Time
e.t: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “do for the third time”. It describes an action repeated until it has occurred three times. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, in passages from 1 Samuel and 1 Kings. The word itself gives the reader a precise sense of repetition, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what action is being repeated. Its meaning is straightforward: something is done again, completing a third occurrence.

This Greek LXX adverb means “beyond measure” or “exceedingly.” It describes something that goes far beyond an ordinary degree or expected limit, intensifying the action, quality, or circumstance it accompanies. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 10:34. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its normal meaning is emphatic: something is present or done to an extraordinary extent.

This Greek LXX verb describes a person as “overly intuitive” or “frantic.” As a verb, it expresses this condition rather than naming a person or object. The available wording does not provide a fuller contextual distinction between the two meanings. In this corpus, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding context, which is not included here.

This verb means to write beneath an inscription or to add writing to something already written. It describes the act of subjoining or appending text rather than beginning an entirely separate document. The word occurs eight times in this Greek corpus, appearing in Esther and several Maccabean writings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being written and what text it accompanies.

Phadassour, also rendered Fathassur, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament wording of Numbers. The name occurs five times, all within Numbers, from Numbers 1:10 through Numbers 10:23. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identifying: it distinguishes a particular person named in Israel’s wilderness-era records, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about that person.

This Greek LXX verb means “trivialize”: to treat something as unimportant, insignificant, or unworthy of serious regard. It describes the act of lowering the value or importance of a person, thing, responsibility, or matter. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 12 verses, so its basic sense is established across several biblical books rather than being limited to one setting. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “friends with; act friendly towards.” It describes behaving toward someone as a friend or treating that person in a friendly way. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times, including passages from Judges, 2 Chronicles, and Sirach. The word expresses an action or attitude directed toward another person, so the surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on friendship itself or on acting in a friendly manner.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a small stone or pebble. It names a physically small piece of rock rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both in Job, so its normal meaning is clear even though it is not widely attested in this corpus. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic word itself points to a small stone or pebble.

This verb means “bring into hand; manage.” It describes taking something into one’s control or handling it. The wording can therefore point to directing, organizing, or dealing with something, while its exact force depends on the sentence where it appears. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. These occurrences belong to the deuterocanonical writings and show that the word is a specific action word rather than a general noun for a person or thing.

Chellēs, also rendered “Khellis,” is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it identifies someone by name. This name occurs five times in four verses within the Old Testament Greek corpus, appearing in 1 Chronicles and 2 Chronicles. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify each named person’s particular role.

This adjective describes something associated with a bridle decorated with gold studs. It points to a bridle’s richly ornamented appearance rather than naming the bridle itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 10:29. Its exact grammatical role in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its central meaning remains clear: having or being furnished with a gold-studded bridle.
